Direct-acting (or “direct‐acting electric”) radiators convert virtually 100 % of the electrical energy they draw into heat at the point of use – in that narrow sense they are “fully efficient.” However, when we look at overall energy efficiency and cost in a building or home, several important factors work against them:

1. Primary energy losses  
   – Electricity generation and distribution typically incurs losses of 30–60 % between the fuel source (coal, gas or renewables) and your plug socket.  
   – By contrast, district heating or modern heat pumps often have lower overall losses and can deliver heat more cheaply per kWh of delivered heat.

2. Operating cost  
   – In most markets the retail price of electricity is two to three times higher than that of natural gas, district heat or biomass.  
   – Running a home primarily on direct electric heat therefore tends to be more expensive, even if the on-site conversion is “100 % efficient.”

An energy declaration (in Swedish “energideklaration”) is an official report—often referred to in English as an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—that describes a building’s energy performance and recommends measures to improve it. It is required by EU regulation (Directive 2010/31/EU) and by Swedish law for most residential and non-residential buildings whenever they are constructed, sold or rented out.  

Key elements of an energy declaration include:  
• Energy Performance Rating  
  – A graded scale (commonly A–G) indicating the building’s overall energy efficiency, based on calculated or measured energy use per square meter and year.  
• Energy Use Breakdown  
  – An account of the building’s energy consumption for heating, cooling, domestic hot water, ventilation and lighting.  
• Building Envelope Characteristics  
  – Information about walls, roofs, windows and doors, including insulation levels and thermal transmittance (U-values).  
• Technical Installations  
  – Descript

Energy‐efficiency improvement refers to any measure or combination of measures that reduces a building’s energy consumption while maintaining or enhancing its functionality and comfort. In practice, this can include:

• Upgrading the building envelope  
  – Adding or improving insulation in walls, roofs and floors  
  – Installing high‐performance windows and doors  
  – Sealing air leaks to improve airtightness  

• Modernizing technical systems  
  – Replacing old boilers, heat pumps, or chillers with more efficient models  
  – Installing advanced ventilation systems with heat recovery  
  – Upgrading lighting to LED or other low-energy alternatives  

• Installing energy‐management and control systems  
  – Smart thermostats, building‐automation systems and sensors that optimize heating, cooling and lighting based on occupancy and weather conditions  

• Incorporating renewable energy sources  
  – Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels, solar thermal collectors or small‐scale wind turbine

Apartment buildings typically employ a combination of envelope-, HVAC- and system-level upgrades to bring down energy use and improve comfort. Common measures include:

1. Improved thermal insulation  
   • External wall insulation (ETICS) or cavity-wall infill  
   • Loft/roof insulation to reduce heat loss upward  
   • Insulated ground-floor or basement slab upgrades  

2. High-performance windows and doors  
   • Triple- or double-glazed units with low-emissivity (low-E) coatings  
   • High-quality frame materials (e.g. thermally broken aluminum, uPVC)  
   • Air-tight seals and weather-stripping to eliminate draughts  

3. Efficient heating, cooling and ventilation  
   • Heat pumps (air-source or ground-source) replacing older boilers  
   • Condensing gas boilers with modulating burners  
   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) to recover 60–90 % of exhaust heat  
   • Smart thermostats and weather-compensated control systems  

4. Lighting and electrical systems

In most residential and small commercial buildings, electricity consumption breaks down roughly into the following major categories (percentages will vary by climate, building type and occupancy):  
1. Space heating and cooling  
   • Electric resistance or heat‐pump systems for space heating often account for 30–50 % of total electricity use in all-electric buildings.  
   • Air‐conditioning or mechanical cooling (where installed) can add another 5–15 % (higher in warmer climates).  

2. Domestic hot water  
   • Electric water heaters or heat‐pump water heaters typically consume 15–25 % of a home’s electricity.  

3. Lighting  
   • General indoor lighting (LED, fluorescent, etc.) represents about 10–15 % of annual use.  

4. Major appliances  
   • Kitchen appliances (refrigerator, freezer, oven, dishwasher) plus laundry machines often total 15–20 %.  

5. Small loads and plug-in devices  
   • Electronics, chargers, TVs, computers and other “plug loads” can account for 5–10 %.

Natural (or “passive”) ventilation—where fresh air is supplied and stale air removed by pressure differences, thermal buoyancy and wind—offers several advantages over fully mechanical systems:

1. Lower energy consumption  
   • No or minimal use of fans and blowers reduces electricity demand.  
   • Passive stack effects and cross-ventilation harness natural forces at no ongoing cost.

2. Reduced operating and maintenance costs  
   • Fewer moving parts (fans, motors, filters) mean less routine service, replacement and repair.  
   • No mechanical components to clean or balance, and no filters to change regularly.

3. Improved indoor environmental quality  
   • Gentle, draft-free airflow can enhance occupant comfort.  
   • Greater opportunity for direct introduction of outdoor air can dilute pollutants effectively.  
   • Acoustic comfort improves because there is no fan noise or vibration.

4. Resilience and simplicity  
   • Still operates during power outages—critical for fire sa

  1. Normal (AC) charging  
     – “Level 1” (slow): 120 V–240 V, roughly 2 kW–3.7 kW (domestic wall-outlet)  
     – “Level 2” (semi-fast): single- or three-phase 230 V–400 V AC, typically up to 7.4 kW, 11 kW or 22 kW  

  2. Fast (DC) charging  
     – Starts at roughly 22 kW–43 kW and is almost always delivered as DC

         • 50 kW DC

         • 150 kW–350 kW DC (“ultra-fast” or “high-power” charging)

Ventilation balancing is the process of measuring, adjusting and fine-tuning the airflows in a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that every room or zone receives exactly the supply and extract airflow rates for which the system was designed. From an energy-use perspective, proper balancing delivers several important benefits:

1. Reduced heating and cooling demand  
   – Over-ventilation (too much fresh air) forces the heating or cooling plant to work harder to bring incoming air to the desired indoor temperature. Balanced flows eliminate excessive air changes and thus lower the thermal load on radiators, heat pumps or air-handling units.  

2. Improved heat-recovery performance  
   – In systems equipped with heat-recovery ventilators (HRV or ERV), matching supply and exhaust rates maximizes the transfer of heat (and, in ERVs, moisture) between outgoing and incoming air streams. This means less energy is required to re-heat or re-cool the fresh air.

Yes. Turning down your indoor thermostat is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to reduce energy consumption, especially in electrically or fuel-heated buildings. Key points:  
• Typical savings: Every degree you lower the set-point during the heating season cuts your heating energy use by roughly 5–7 percent.  
• Comfort and health: A living-room temperature of 20 °C and bedrooms at 16–18 °C are generally considered comfortable while still delivering good savings.  
• Time-of-day setbacks: Use a programmable or smart thermostat to automatically drop the temperature when you sleep or are away, then raise it again shortly before you return or wake up.
